I've also had systems that invert this and allow cheaper models to call out to more capable models when they need to, but in my observation I found them quite bad at knowing even when to call out and I find wrapping the cheap models a bit more reliable in that problems tend to get caught before they bubble up to the user.

My bandaid fix for this is having a large number of sessions or "agents" and being ok with them being inactive at times, but they maintain their context. This has to be in some kind of system with appropriately sized "departments" to justify that agent's existence, or to justify it splitting into two, or creating sub-agents, etc. Yes, there is a cost when you cold start an agent after a week, but for now I'd rather pull that whole 400k+ context back without layers and layers of /compact. And then hopefully you keep that agent going for long enough to benefit from any cache-hit discounts.

Not really a good analogy, but it feels like having an image you like but every time you view it, it runs it through another loop of jpg compression. Use it when it's most effective, otherwise let it preserve it's details.

I too feel like context management has a lot of room for improvement, but the problem right now is that dynamic context management will most likely tank your cache hit rate. We need caching that's not just based on prefix-matching for this to make sense.

children.author: jcims
angry_octet
children.text:
Exactly, there is no perfect process for such simplistic binary decision making. But we are seeing pipelines for tasks, like document processing, where it is becoming accepted that the machine is right.

Rather than binary classification we should be locating document fragments in a high dimensional feature space, and with all those fragments coming to a confidence bounded guess.

Additionally, when someone submits documents that can't be recognised as valid, the response should not be INVALID, it should be UNDECIDED. In that sense, passing to Opus is great, but passing a tiny fragment of the problem is a bad way to do it.

>Is this model going to return confidence values? No, they want decisions.

The system doesn't return confidence values because that's not what they are designing. The models, however, do and to me it's interesting that Jev's measure of confidence is pretty well calibrated to its correctness.

>Without knowing the cultural context, the location, the document type, the document author, etc, you could be getting it wrong.

And? There's no perfect process, just ones that asymptotically approach correctness at exponentially increasing cost. They own the system and get to decide what works for them.

It's illustrative that there are even errors in how the humans have formulated the task and documented the errors.

They propose:

Valentino → Female Child

Yet this is obviously a boy name, else it would be Valentina. Is this model going to return confidence values? No, they want decisions. This is an inherent problem in AI with reductive logic for these tasks.

Likewise, dates. Is 17/08/22:

- 20170822 (Chinese write the year first, and in speech and chat they will say '17' not '2017'.)

- 20220817 (Everywhere But North America.)

Is 04/06/2009:

- 20090604 (Non-North American)

- 20090406 (American)

Without knowing the cultural context, the location, the document type, the document author, etc, you could be getting it wrong.

children.text:
Yep. It's actually kind of mind blowing how well "reasoning" works at de-biasing and pushing out of global minima, in hindsight, when you see how jagged things get again without.

These are the results of a little performance tuning/permutation testing run against context format and question wording we did. Obviously there is a lot of noise here but I was actually kinda surprised that there was a clear "best way to ask the question" even for relatively low N and low complexity/ambiguity of the task.

(This is a ~30s Ai-driven gif presentation of the results, the full grid shows up about 15s in): https://imgur.com/a/wGFZvGw

These models in particular have some pretty dubiously generalized and diverse training datasets. You can see this for yourself BTW by looking at the datasets SOTA Jev-like models are being trained against and evaluated on. children.text: Yeah, it’s a precision/recall tradeoff. And as such you calibrate by the cost of each FP vs FN.

It's not a problem you can get right, because you can't know if you need to escalate until after you escalate (and what you escalated to disagrees with what your first choice would have been). But that's the point: how cautious you make the model is the knob that lets your trade cost for correctness.

I don't believe the answer is ever "how certain is the model?" It's "how much is at stake?" Or "how hard of a problem does this appear to be?" It's not about teaching the model to have uncertainty, but rather to be avoidant of things that are sufficiently important to get right.

This is the Model Router architecture, from another angle. The problem is always, how does a dumb model know it needs to escalate to a smart model?

Some problems are obviously hard known-unknowns (eg “solve Navier Stokes”). The problem is unknown-unknowns or knowledge gaps, where the model doesn’t know they need help.
